newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says ready to go it alone on refinery.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says ready to go it alone on refinery.

text.p: Vietnam will press ahead with construction of its first oil refinery without foreign partners, a senior official of the state oil and gas firm Petrovietnam said on Monday.

"Our government has decided to authorise Petrovietnam to build the refinery," Vu Van Mao, Director of Petrovietnam's Petroleum Information Centre, told reporters at an energy industry conference. "It will be built by Petrovietnam only."
He said the government was urging Petrovietnam to finish a feasibility study for the $1.3 billion refinery quickly and get it built by the turn of the century.
The Saigon Times Daily on Monday quoted Petrovietnam President Ngo Thuong San as saying that finding capital for the project was not an "unsolvable problem".
The government's plan to build the refinery in Dung Quat, an undeveloped area 1,000 km (600 miles) north of the country's oilfields and chief consumption base, has been highly controversial.
The French oil firm Total SA withdrew from the 6.5-million-tonne-per year refinery project in 1995, branding it economically unviable.
A group of foreign oil majors, which was put together to replace Total, was disbanded after its feasibility study was rejected by Petrovietnam.

The consortium companies had asked for a chance to compete at the distribution and retail level on their own or in a joint venture with local firms and, according to one source, had asked for guaranteed prices for refinery products.
San told the Saigon Times Daily that Vietnam was cooperating with foreign consultancy service companies to seek both foreign and domestic capital for the project.
"Quite a few foreign financial consultancy companies have expressed their intention to help Petrovietnam borrow foreign capital, but we will look at local sources first," he said.
He said Petrovietnam's accumulated capital would meet some 30 percent of the total investment needed.

San said that for 1997, Petrovietnam had been granted permission to use 30 percent of its share of profits from the Vietsovpetro venture with Russia and from 1998 it would be entitled to take all of its profit of around $150 million a year.

The newspaper quoted San as saying the investment needed for the refinery would be cut by $350 million through a plan to use sulphur-free crude from Vietnam's White Tiger oilfield instead of partially relying on crude from the Middle East.
He said the main concern was a lack of local technicians and experts to operate the project and added that United States-based Fosterwheele had been invited to act as technical consultant.
